value.estimate: 2-4 days to reproduce the architecture on a catalog you already have; weeks to earn the numbers
value.why: The scored path is stdlib Python with no model, so the retrieval, ranking, slate shaping and question selection logic is legible in a day and the harness is in the repo. What does not come free is the evaluator and the catalog statistics it leans on - popularity priors, attribute lead lines and rare-phrase evidence are all derived from that specific 50,000-product dump.

data_and_models.value: No trained model in the scored path. Retrieval is BM25 over the supplied 50,000-product catalog with a shared regex tokenizer and 31-word stopword list, a popularity prior ln(1+rating_number), a rare-phrase evidence index, and an optional dense asset that the design documents as rejected at weight zero. Scoring is a fixed convex combination of HitRate@10, MRR and an efficiency term derived from mean turns to conversion.

how_it_works.value: Python standard library only, all in memory, no external call on the scored path. At construction (about 5.6 s and 280 MB peak) it builds coarse category buckets for hard filtering, a BM25 index whose regex word tokenizer and 31-word stopword list are the identical function used for indexing and for queries, a popularity prior ln(1+rating_number), an attribute vocabulary with lead lines for question scoring, and a rare-phrase index for per-product evidence. A dense vector asset is built optionally and then rejected at weight zero. The turn path is parse, fold state, select behaviour, retrieve, rank, shape slate, choose or suppress question, recovery check, then response plus session trace. Files named on the page include submission/src/text.py, with evaluator/ and harness/ directories alongside.

how_they_tested.value: test modules present in the linked repository — harness/tests/__init__.py, harness/tests/fixtures.py, harness/tests/test_analysis.py, harness/tests/test_deviations.py — which is what the page's harness figures were produced with; the page itself describes no further evaluation protocol

limits_they_disclosed.value: The two decisions they defend are restraint ones. The tokenizer is deliberately not learned and not subword, because one shared function means an indexing choice can never disagree with a lookup choice. The dense retrieval asset is included in the architecture and given weight zero, documented as rejected rather than quietly dropped. The objective itself is the hardest part: the 0.30 reciprocal-rank term is what makes slate width a real decision, since exposing ten products immediately improves turns-to-conversion while hurting rank enough to lower the combined score.

value.relation: same genre - an agent pipeline that reports a measured before/after with a cost figure - but the two sit at opposite ends of auditability: Greenlight's numbers are asserted with a stated cost ladder and no harness, SATU's can be recomputed from the formula on the page and its harness is in the linked repository.

what_breaks_first.value: The evaluator's proxy. Optimising 'the session ends when the target appears in the slate' rewards wide early slates and precise question-baiting, which is not the same thing as a shopper being helped; HitRate@10 of 1.000 with 2.27 turns says the target was surfaced, not that the other nine products were good or that the user trusted the answer. Second: state robustness - typed slots, refusals and an exhaustion path are all deterministic logic over a 50k catalog, and the page reports no adversarial or human sessions to show the behaviour selection recovering from a shopper who changes their mind.

what_it_does.value: Takes a shopper message per turn and returns a slate of products plus optionally one clarification question. Six behaviours are selected from state (discovery, precision, recovery, boundary, stagnation, coverage); retrieval narrows to an active category with hard filters, ranking orders the candidates, slate shaping decides how many products to expose now, question selection either offers the most informative attribute probe or suppresses the question, and a recovery check watches for a shopper who has been shown everything relevant. Each turn is ~1 ms and every number the page quotes is derived from a published harness.

what_it_is.value: A deterministic stateful shopping agent for a 50,000-product catalog that treats recommendation as a sequential decision problem, choosing both slate width and whether to ask another question, and reports a recomputable score against a BM25 baseline.

what_to_steal.value: Publish the objective function next to the results, including how failures are counted, so the number can be checked rather than trusted; make the expensive optional component visible at weight zero instead of deleting it, which documents a decision and its cost; use one shared preprocessing function for index and query; and treat 'how many items do I show now' and 'is another question worth a turn' as two explicit, stateful decisions rather than fixed constants.

satu.name: SATU: Shopping Assistant That Understands
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.86, zero unknowns, 100% of the rubric was checkable → strong
satu.worth_note: Not for the score - for the discipline. A hackathon team published the objective, the metric definitions, the convention for misses, and a baseline row, then made every design decision answerable to it: slate width as a real variable because reciprocal rank is weighted, the dense asset kept in the architecture at weight zero and labelled rejected, one tokenizer shared by index and query so the two can never disagree. It is the rare submission where a reader can recompute the headline number from the page, and the arithmetic closes to four decimals.

value.estimate: 5-7 weeks for a single-jurisdiction version a buyer would trust; a year of data work for the catalog that makes it worth using
value.why: The application is ordinary: photo preprocessing with Sharp, a queue on Inngest, Prisma over Postgres, Next.js and Stripe, and a multimodal model call with search grounding for part numbers and live prices - two or three weeks for someone fluent in that stack. The time goes into the parts catalog and the pricing source, which are the only defensible parts of the product and are not built here at all: structuring OEM data per make, model and year, keeping prices from becoming stale, and deciding what to return when coverage is thin. Adding a second jurisdiction (ECE instead of DOT/SAE, EUR, per-country import and inspection rules) is a further multiplier rather than a config flag. A clone can reproduce the flow quickly; it cannot reproduce the asset.

data_and_models.value: Two vendor capabilities and one internal asset: Gemini 2.5 Flash, Pro and Flash-Lite via @google/genai for the multimodal read (with automatic failover between the three), Google Search grounding for OEM part-number lookup and live price verification, and a proprietary parts catalog the page sizes at 700,000-plus records across 60-plus makes. Prisma plus PostgreSQL hold estimates and users, Inngest runs the pipeline, R2 or Supabase hold images, Sharp normalises them before inference. No model is trained, and no accuracy, precision or price-error figure is published for either the vision step or the grounding step - the numbers on the page are throughput (under 2 minutes), asset size (700,000 records, 60-plus makes) and band edges (40 and 70 percent), not measurement.

how_it_works.value: Next.js App Router with TypeScript, Tailwind and React on the front; Prisma over PostgreSQL (Neon) for state, Cloudflare R2 or Supabase for media, Sharp for image preparation, and Inngest for the asynchronous estimate pipeline. Stripe carries multi-currency billing. Recognition and pricing run on Gemini 2.5 Flash, Pro and Flash-Lite through @google/genai, with automatic failover between the three models, and Google Search grounding is used to look up OEM part numbers and verify live prices. Nothing is trained; the parts catalog the page calls proprietary, at 700,000-plus records across 60-plus vehicle makes, is presented as an asset rather than as something built here, and its construction is not documented.

how_they_tested.value: No evaluation of any kind is described: no precision or recall on part identification, no back-test of repair estimates against shop invoices or auction outcomes, no error bars on the Loss Ratio, no hold-out by make or model year, and no mention of a test suite. The only quantitative structure on the page is the Loss Ratio band policy - Low under 40 percent, Moderate 40 to 70, High above 70 - which is a threshold choice presented as matching 'EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation for either standard. The honesty device the page does describe is in the interface rather than in a benchmark: scarcity detection and advisory banners that flag where the catalog does not reach.

limits_they_disclosed.value: Coverage is the stated problem, and the page treats it as a design constraint rather than an edge case: it describes scarcity detection and advisory banners whose job is to communicate the limits of the parts catalog honestly instead of returning empty or misleading results, with the operating principle stated plainly - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than showing no result. The second named difficulty is jurisdiction: two standards bodies, two currencies, and per-country import, title, emissions and inspection rules that have to be attached to the right estimate rather than translated after the fact, which is also what pulls Stripe multi-currency into the stack.

value.relation: both turn a stream of sensor evidence into a regulatory-flavoured verdict for a human to act on, and neither page publishes an accuracy figure - the fisheries tool goes further and states there is no ground truth for its risk classification, while Carbender's page implies its bands come from external standards without naming them. Read together, they are the two failure modes of the same design: admit the measurement problem, or borrow authority from a regulator.

both end in an artifact a person checks rather than an action the system takes - a repair plan PDF against a cited diff - and both leave the accuracy of the underlying judgement unmeasured. The difference is what they attach evidence to: Continuity grounds a claim against the live web and shows the citation next to the verdict, while Carbender grounds a part number against a proprietary catalog the reader cannot inspect, so its traceability stops at the vendor boundary.

both put a machine-readable judgement in front of a purchase decision and both monetise through the transaction surface rather than the model; the marketplace tool's advantage is that its output is checked by the market on the next listing, whereas a repair estimate is only checked when the parts arrive, so the feedback loop is months long.

what_breaks_first.value: Catalog coverage, on both ends of the pipeline. The 700,000-row figure is spread over 60-plus makes and their model years, so the first user with a twelve-year-old European hatchback gets either no parts or a plausible wrong code - and the scarcity banner only helps if scarcity is detected against coverage the product actually measures rather than against a lookup that happens to miss. Second, the severity-to-cost link: the bands assume the repair estimate is close enough to divide by resale value, and near 40 and 70 percent a modest error in labour or parts changes 'repairable' into 'Total Loss' with no stated error model to tell the buyer which side of the line they are on. Third, spatial normalisation: the driver-side versus passenger-side disambiguation is the difference between quoting a mirror or a fender, and a cropped, low-light auction photo is precisely where a 3D-normalisation step degrades.

what_it_does.value: Photos go in and a structured estimate comes out: damaged parts identified against an OEM catalog, each graded Severe, Moderate or Cosmetic, with 3D spatial normalisation used to tell driver-side from passenger-side damage rather than trusting the photo's left and right. Every identified part carries a real-market price report, and the parts assemble into a Repair Planner that exports a PDF. A Loss Ratio - Total Estimated Repair Cost divided by Clean Market Resale Value - is banded Low under 40 percent, Moderate 40 to 70, High above 70, described as matching EU and US salvage threshold standards, and a High ratio returns a Total Loss verdict. Jurisdiction changes the vocabulary (US DOT/SAE standards and USD, EU ECE in EUR) and adds country-aware import, title, emissions and inspection warnings. A separate free tool at carbender.com/window-sticker turns a VIN into a Monroney window sticker, and the whole product is a zero-download mobile web app in four locales (English, Lithuanian, Polish and US English).

what_it_is.value: A salvage-buyer's tool that turns damage photos into a priced OEM parts list, grades severity panel by panel, and divides the repair estimate by clean resale value to say whether the car is worth fixing at all - with US and EU rulebooks treated as different products, and missing parts coverage announced instead of papered over.

what_to_steal.value: Publish the decision rule, not just the score: the Loss Ratio names both inputs, states the band edges, and returns a verdict - a reader can recompute it and argue with it, which is more than most 'AI estimate' products offer. Then steal the failure-surface design: scarcity detection wired to an advisory banner, with the explicit principle that admitting no coverage beats a confident wrong answer. Region should be an input, not a translation - standards family, currency and title/import/emissions/inspection rules change what the estimate means, so carry them through the model call and the UI together. Free adjacent utility as acquisition: a VIN-to-window-sticker generator that costs nothing to run and lands the same audience on the paid product. And three model tiers with automatic failover in a flow running against an auction clock.

hazard.note: This is a money decision dressed in regulatory vocabulary. The product returns a Total Loss verdict and a repair estimate that a buyer may bid against, while invoking DOT, SAE and ECE standards, country-specific import, title, emissions and inspection requirements, and a Loss Ratio band policy described as 'matching EU & US salvage threshold standards' with no citation and no named issuing body for either threshold. Nothing on the page states who is liable when the estimate is wrong, no accuracy figure exists for either the part identification or the price, and the resale denominator comes from another estimate rather than a transaction record, so a High-band verdict near a boundary can flip on inputs that are both soft. The team's stated posture is the right instinct - a wrong OEM code shown with false confidence is worse than no result - but an interface banner is not a compliance sign-off, and a tool that names regulators should either cite them or stop invoking them. Held from promotion on that basis: publishable as a documented case, not as a usable figure.

carbender.name: Carbender
verdict_reasons: soundness 0.57 over 64% of the rubric; 0 named unknown(s) remain → publishable with caveats
carbender.worth_note: The audience is specific and it pays: people bidding on salvage lots, body shops and mechanics, for whom a photo-to-parts-list-with-prices replaces a guess made in a ten-minute walk-around. Within that audience the wedge is real and better than the obvious alternative, because the two things a human estimator cannot do at an auction - check a 700,000-row OEM catalog and price parts across a jurisdiction boundary - are exactly what the build automates, and the Loss Ratio turns a pile of numbers into the one decision the buyer came with. What keeps it niche rather than strong is that the mechanism does not outlive the project: vision plus grounded pricing plus a published decision ratio is a well-executed instance of a pattern that will be repeated, and the moat is the catalog, not the method. No accuracy figure anywhere means a buyer inherits the author's confidence rather than a measured one - which the page at least admits is the wrong thing to hand over, hence the scarcity banners.
